summary: Specifies the HEMS Monitoring and Control Language, which defines the requests and replies used in HEMS. It assumes knowledge of RFC 1021 and ASN.1. It was replaced by RFC 1076.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the list of questions you can ask a machine and the kinds of answers it gives back in a management system.

what control operations does hems support
subtitle: A query language for monitoring and controlling network entities.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a uniform way to query the status of various network devices and entities, and sometimes to control them remotely.
tldr.mechanism: HEMS defines a query language using a stack-based approach with opcodes that operate on hierarchical data structures represented in ASN.1 format. Queries and responses use templates and tags to retrieve specific data from monitored entities.
tldr.outcome: This version was replaced by RFC 1076, which provided improvements to the monitoring and control system.

today: RFC 1023 specified an experimental monitoring and control language for HEMS, published in October 1987. This version was superseded by RFC 1076, which provided an updated and improved specification for HEMS Monitoring and Control Language.

sections.title: Introduction to HEMS Monitoring and Control
sections.content:
RFC 1023 specifies the HEMS Monitoring and Control Language, a general-purpose language for managing network entities such as gateways and routers. HEMS is part of the High-Level Entity Monitoring System described in RFC 1021 and RFC 1022. The language defines how to send queries to a monitored entity and receive responses, using the ISO standard ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation 1) data encoding rules.

A query is a complete request that stands on its own and elicits a complete response, with no notion of an interactive conversation. The data in a monitored entity is modeled as a hierarchy, with specific items named by the path from the root to the item of interest. Most items are read-only, but some can be set to perform control operations. Both requests and responses are represented using ASN.1.
sections.plainLanguage: HEMS lets you ask a computer questions about itself (like how many packets it has received) using a structured format, and it gives you answers in the same structured format. You can also use it to give the computer commands.

sections.title: Hierarchical Data Model
sections.content:
Data in a monitored entity is organized as a hierarchy where each node represents a piece of information or a collection of similar items. The hierarchy offers useful structure for organization, naming, mapping onto ASN.1, and efficient representation. Each node in the hierarchy has names for its component parts, usually represented as small integers (typically less than 100) called ASN.1 tags, which can be mapped to the entity's internal representation.

An internal node in the hierarchy is called a dictionary. A dictionary is a container for related data items, such as system information, interfaces, processes, routing tables, and ARP tables. A special type of dictionary called an array contains only one type of item repeated multiple times. For example, an interfaces array might contain multiple interface entries, each with the same structure.

Data is named by specifying the path through the hierarchy from the root. For instance, the name of a routing table entry's destination would be route-table{ route-entry{ dest } }. When data is not available (either because it is not defined or does not apply in a particular situation), it is returned as a zero-length data item rather than generating an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The data is organized like a file cabinet: at the top is a drawer (the root), which contains folders (dictionaries) like 'system' and 'interfaces', and each folder contains files (data items). You get to an item by naming the path from the cabinet to the file.

sections.title: Query Language and Core Operations
sections.content:
The HEMS query language is not a programming language but a stack-based system of operations. The central element is a stack that may contain templates, data, or dictionaries. Initially, the stack contains the root dictionary. As the query is processed, ASN.1 objects that are not opcodes are pushed onto the stack, while each opcode is executed immediately and may generate output.

The primary operations are: GET emits an ASN.1 object with the same shape as a given template, returning zero-length items for data that does not exist; BEGIN pushes a sub-dictionary onto the stack and starts an ASN.1 object; END terminates an ASN.1 object and pops the dictionary; and GET-MATCH selects array entries based on matching field values rather than numeric indices.

The language supports a GET-ATTRIBUTES operation that returns descriptive information about data items (such as long descriptions, short descriptions, units, and precision) so that clients can understand the meaning of data without relying on external documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The query language works like a simple command system: you put things on a stack, give it commands (like 'GET this' or 'BEGIN that'), and it sends you back answers. It does not have fancy programming features, just enough to ask questions and get answers.

sections.title: Control Operations and Data Modification
sections.content:
Beyond retrieving data, the HEMS language allows modification through the SET operation, which changes values of data in the monitored entity. Control operations that do not correspond to simply changing a value (such as bringing an interface up or down) are represented as setting a special command-code item to an appropriate value.

The SET-MATCH operation modifies data in array entries that match specified values, similar to GET-MATCH but for writing instead of reading. The CREATE operation inserts a new entry into an array, while the DELETE operation removes entries that match specified values. These operations allow network administrators to perform administrative tasks remotely, such as disabling an interface with a particular IP address or deleting routing table entries.

The language also provides GET-RANGE for retrieving ranges of data, primarily useful for examining memory at specific address ranges. This supports low-level remote debugging operations when necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides asking questions, you can give commands to change things: SET changes a value, CREATE adds a new item, and DELETE removes an item. You can target specific items by their values, so you can say 'find the interface with this IP address and turn it off' without knowing its number.

sections.title: Error Handling and Data Validation
sections.content:
The HEMS protocol handles errors gracefully. When requested data is not available (either because it is not defined or not applicable), it is returned as a zero-length value rather than generating an error. This allows completely generic queries to be composed without regard to whether the data is defined at all entities that will receive the request.

When actual errors occur (such as improper arguments on the stack or attempting to begin on a non-dictionary), an ERROR object is emitted. Since multiple ASN.1 objects may be open at the time an error occurs, each unterminated object is closed with a copy of the ERROR object. After all open objects are terminated, a final copy of the ERROR object is emitted. This structure ensures that the error is noticed at every level of interpretation on the receiving end.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for something that does not exist, HEMS just gives you back an empty answer instead of complaining. But if something goes really wrong (like bad syntax), it sends an error message that gets wrapped in all the open structures so you do not miss it.

sections.title: Extensions and Vendor-Specific Data
sections.content:
The RFC provides two methods for extending HEMS to support new data types. The preferred method is to register the new data and its meaning, then get an official ASN.1 tag assigned, making the specification available to everyone. The second method uses a VendorSpecific application type to wrap vendor-specific data that does not have standard numbers assigned. For example, if a vendor has interface-related data that does not fit into the standard schema, it can wrap it in a VendorSpecific container with its own internal tag assignments.

If the vendor-specific method is used, complete descriptions must be available through the GET-ATTRIBUTES and GET-ATTRIBUTES-MATCH operations so that clients can understand the meaning of the non-standard data. The RFC notes that while this extensibility mechanism is provided, registering standard tags is the preferred approach because it makes the data specification available for broader reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: HEMS can be extended with new types of data. The proper way is to register them officially, but vendors can also wrap custom data in a special VendorSpecific box and provide descriptions so others can understand it.
